candidates.attacker_control: An attacker who supplies a malicious CGMES ZIP controls ZIP entry names and entry contents. Entry names such as one containing '..' segments or an absolute path are returned verbatim by ZipArchiveDataSource.listNames(); CgmesOnDataSource.names() retains them if they end in .xml/.zip and the entry starts with a root element carrying RDF and CIM namespaces. The same attacker-controlled name is then used as the destination filename.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: CgmesOnDataSource.names() does impose two constraints: names must end in .xml/.zip and must parse at least a root element with valid RDF/CIM namespaces. These do not prevent traversal, and an attacker controls entry contents. The sink is only a direct filesystem write when the destination DataSource is DirectoryDataSource or another filesystem-backed implementation; MemDataSource and archive-backed targets do not immediately write outside files. The repository contains no in-tree call to Importer.copy/CgmesImport.copy, so standard CLI reachability is unproven. No tests were run and no exploit was attempted.
candidates.impact: An attacker-controlled ZIP entry name can cause creation or truncation of a file outside the destination directory, within paths writable by the process. The suffix restriction limits targets to .xml and .zip paths, but configuration XML, deployment/data archives, or other sensitive XML/ZIP files can be overwritten, causing data corruption, configuration tampering, denial of service, and potentially follow-on compromise if the overwritten file is later consumed by the application. Code execution is not established.
candidates.prerequisites: A downstream application must invoke Importer.copy or CgmesImport.copy with an untrusted ReadOnlyDataSource (typically a ZIP created via DataSource.fromPath) and a filesystem-backed target DataSource, normally DirectoryDataSource. The process must have write permission to the intended path, and the target path must be an existing parent for a .xml/.zip file. No in-repository caller of copy was found.
candidates.root_cause: CgmesImport.copy iterates names returned from CgmesOnDataSource.names() and passes each raw name as both source and destination to copyStream. The names originate from ZIP entry metadata and are only checked for a .xml/.zip suffix and RDF/CIM namespaces; neither '..' segments nor absolute paths are rejected. copyStream then calls to.newOutputStream(toName, false), and DirectoryDataSource.getPath resolves that name directly against its directory and opens it with CREATE/TRUNCATE. This lets the entry name escape the destination DataSource directory.
candidates.title: CGMES copy preserves attacker-controlled ZIP entry paths, allowing file writes outside the destination
candidates.trace: CgmesImport.copy constructs CgmesOnDataSource(from).names() (lines 407-414). names() calls dataSource.listNames(REGEX_VALID_NAME) and removes only entries that do not exist or lack RDF/CIM namespaces (lines 82-90), while the regex only enforces an .xml/.zip suffix (lines 138-144). ZipArchiveDataSource.listNames returns raw archive entry names (lines 192-208). copy() passes each raw name to copyStream(from, to, name, name) (line 414), and copyStream calls to.newOutputStream(toName, false) (lines 600-607). For DirectoryDataSource, getPath returns directory.resolve(fileName) without normalization or containment verification, and newOutputStream opens it with create/truncate semantics (lines 83-98).
candidates.unverified: The candidate is not runtime-confirmed. The downstream copy API usage, upload/file-naming behavior, destination DataSource type, process permissions, and exact writable targets were not observed. The source-relation index cannot prove data flow or reachability. There may be unreviewed callers outside this repository.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22: Path Traversal / Zip Slip-style arbitrary file write

coverage_summary: Reviewed the full model-visible scope for this run: 2,923 source files. I focused on security-sensitive areas including commons datasources/archives/XML/config, CGMES import/export/completion/model and triplestore handling, computation-local process and archive handling, math serialization, Groovy scripting, and distributed security-analysis file handling. The P1 relation index covers 2,887 files with 2,382 Java files; 36 source files are missing from the index, and the index supports only syntax-level navigation, not control/data flow or semantic resolution. This was a targeted broad review, not a line-by-line audit of every file.
limitations: No build, tests, scanners, or exploit payloads were executed; the finding is not runtime-confirmed.
The selected CGMES copy path has no in-repository caller, so exposure depends on downstream application usage and the attacker's ability to supply a malicious CGMES ZIP.
Impact is limited to .xml/.zip destination names and to paths writable by the process; the destination must be a filesystem-backed DataSource.
The relation index omits 36 files and does not provide data-flow, control-flow, runtime reachability, or complete semantic resolution; Groovy and non-Java behavior may be underrepresented.
No external application, deployment configuration, upload naming scheme, or privilege model was available, so concrete exploitability and any follow-on RCE remain unverified.

rejected_leads.lead: LocalComputationManager ARCHIVE_UNZIP copies every archive entry to workingDir.resolve(ze.getName()) without checking containment
rejected_leads.reason: The missing check is real and allows Zip Slip if a caller creates an InputFile with ARCHIVE_UNZIP and supplies a malicious archive. However, no in-repository producer of an ARCHIVE_UNZIP input file was found, so its reachability is weaker than the selected CGMES copy path.

rejected_leads.lead: SparseMatrix.read uses ObjectInputStream.readObject on the supplied stream
rejected_leads.reason: This is unsafe Java deserialization and a plausible CWE-502 sink, but no in-repository caller passes an untrusted file or stream to it. Treating the presence of the public API alone as exploitable would exceed the source evidence.

rejected_leads.lead: UnixLocalCommandExecutor and WindowsLocalCommandExecutor interpolate args and environment values into shell command strings
rejected_leads.reason: Metacharacters are not escaped, so command injection is possible for callers that supply attacker-controlled args or environment values. The in-repository command builders generally use fixed or internally generated paths/IDs, and no concrete untrusted-to-shell path was established.

rejected_leads.lead: Groovy DSL loaders evaluate scripts from files or streams
rejected_leads.reason: Groovy execution is an intentional scripting feature and is expected to have full code execution by design. No source evidence showed an unintended trust-boundary crossing where ordinary untrusted data is evaluated as a script.

rejected_leads.lead: CreateMissingContainersPreProcessor builds a destination path from a URI authority derived from the CGMES basename
rejected_leads.reason: Percent-encoded separators and URI authority decoding could make the fixes filename escape its configured folder, but exploiting this depends on JDK URI decoding semantics, attacker influence over the baseline, the preprocessor being enabled, and a configured fixes folder. It was not selected without stronger confirmation.

summary: The strongest source-level lead is a Zip-Slip-style path traversal in the CGMES importer copy path. CgmesImport.copy takes archive entry names from CgmesOnDataSource.names() and passes them unchanged to DataSource.newOutputStream(); CgmesOnDataSource only requires a .xml/.zip suffix and valid RDF/CIM namespaces, and DirectoryDataSource then resolves the name directly under its target directory without containment checks. A downstream application that calls Importer.copy/CgmesImport.copy with an untrusted CGMES ZIP and a filesystem-backed destination can therefore overwrite or create files outside the intended directory. No in-tree caller of copy was found, so this remains an API-level candidate rather than a runtime-confirmed issue.
